# How viruses are built and copy themselves

> *A virus particle carries no machinery for making energy or protein. Its structure is a delivery
> system for a genome, and its replication cycle uses the host cell for everything else.*

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Learning objectives
- Describe the parts of a virion, and distinguish enveloped from non-enveloped viruses.
- Predict from its envelope how readily a virus is inactivated outside the host.
- List the six steps of the replication cycle, and distinguish release by budding from release by
  lysis.
- Explain how a DNA virus, a positive-sense RNA virus, a negative-sense RNA virus and a retrovirus
  each make mRNA, and place influenza virus and HIV in this scheme.
- Explain why the enzymes a virus brings or encodes, and not the host machinery it uses, are the
  basis of selective toxicity against viruses.
:::

## The virion {#sec-vstr-virion}

### Parts of a virion {#sec-vstr-structure}

A virion, the virus particle outside a cell, is a genome packaged for delivery to a new cell (see
[*The microbial world*](../foundations/microbial-world.qmd#sec-world-kinds)). It has no ribosomes,
no mitochondria and no enzymes for making ATP, so it does nothing until it enters a cell whose
machinery it can use. Every virion has two parts, and some have a third:

- The genome is DNA or RNA, never both. It carries the genes for the virion's own proteins and, in
  many viruses, for enzymes that copy the genome.
- The **capsid** is a protein shell, built from many copies of one or a few viral proteins, that
  encloses and protects the genome.
- The **envelope**, present in some viruses, is a lipid bilayer around the capsid. The virus takes
  the bilayer from a membrane of the cell in which it was made, and inserts its own proteins into it.

A virus with an envelope is **enveloped**; a virus whose outer surface is the capsid is
**non-enveloped**. Either way, proteins on the outer surface bind the virion to a new host cell.

::: {.concept-tree}
[Parts of a virion]{.tree-title}

- Virion
  - Genome: DNA or RNA
    - DNA: usually double-stranded
    - RNA: usually single-stranded; positive-sense or negative-sense; one molecule or several
      segments
  - Capsid: a protein shell around the genome
  - Envelope, in enveloped viruses only: a lipid bilayer from a host membrane, carrying viral
    proteins
:::

A genome divided into several separate molecules is a **segmented genome**. When two strains of a
segmented virus infect the same cell, new virions can package segments from both, which is one way
influenza viruses change (see [*How viruses change*](virus-change.qmd#sec-vchg-reassortment)).

::: {.example}
The influenza virion is enveloped, and its genome is single-stranded RNA in eight segments. Its
envelope carries two viral proteins: **haemagglutinin**, which binds the virion to airway epithelial
cells, and **neuraminidase**, an enzyme that frees new virions from the cell that made them.
:::

Virions are much smaller than cells. An influenza virion is about 100 nm across, roughly a tenth the
diameter of *Staphylococcus aureus* and below the resolution of the light microscope (see the size
ladder in [*The microbial world*](../foundations/microbial-world.qmd#sec-world-scale)). A particle
this small holds a genome of few genes, and the virus relies on the host cell for its ribosomes, its energy and
most of its enzymes.

### Enveloped and non-enveloped viruses {#sec-vstr-envelope}

The envelope is a lipid membrane and has the weaknesses of one. Drying, detergents, alcohol and bile
disrupt it, and a virion that loses its envelope loses the proteins it needs to attach to a cell, so
it can no longer infect. A capsid without an envelope is a protein shell that withstands these
conditions much better. Enveloped viruses therefore lie at the easily inactivated end of the
resistance spectrum, and non-enveloped viruses further along it (see [*Detecting and controlling
microbes*](../foundations/detection-control.qmd#sec-det-resistance)).

Three consequences follow from the difference:

- Enveloped viruses survive poorly outside the host, and most spread by respiratory particles, blood,
  sexual contact or close contact, which carry them quickly from one host to the next.
- Many non-enveloped viruses survive for long periods on hands, surfaces, food and water, and
  withstand stomach acid and bile, so many spread by the faecal–oral route.
- Alcohol hand rub inactivates enveloped viruses readily. Against non-enveloped viruses, washing with
  soap and water, which removes them physically, is more reliable.

::: {.example}
Alcohol hand rub inactivates influenza virus on hands by disrupting its envelope. Norovirus, a
non-enveloped virus that causes vomiting and diarrhoea, is less reliably inactivated by alcohol, so
hands are washed with soap and water during norovirus outbreaks.
:::

Find the property that explains the difference in survival before the explanation appears.

<div data-island="contrast-pair" data-src="/diagrams/pair-enveloped-nonenveloped.yml"></div>

## The replication cycle {#sec-vstr-cycle}

A bacterium grows and divides in two by binary fission (see [*How bacteria are built and get
energy*](../bacteria/bacteria-build-energy.qmd#sec-bact-growth)). A virus multiplies differently: the
virion comes apart inside a host cell, the cell makes viral parts separately, and many new virions
are assembled from those parts. Every virus passes through the same six steps.

::: {.flow}
1. Attachment
2. Entry
3. Uncoating
4. Genome expression and copying
5. Assembly
6. Release
:::

1. In **attachment**, a protein on the virion surface binds a specific receptor on the host cell,
   which sets the cells the virus can infect, its tropism (see [*Microbes and their
   hosts*](../foundations/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-steps)).
2. In **entry**, the virion gets into the cell, either by fusion of its envelope with the plasma
   membrane or by endocytosis.
3. In **uncoating**, the capsid comes apart and releases the genome inside the cell.
4. In **genome expression and copying**, the virus makes mRNA, which the cell's ribosomes translate
   into viral proteins, and viral or host enzymes make new copies of the genome.
5. In **assembly**, new copies of the genome are packaged into new capsids.
6. In **release**, new virions leave the cell, by budding or by lysis.

Enveloped viruses leave by **budding**. Viral envelope proteins collect in a patch of host membrane,
the capsid pushes out through it, and the membrane closes behind it, so the virion leaves wrapped in
an envelope taken from the cell. Budding does not by itself break the cell open, and a cell can
release virions for some time before it dies. Many non-enveloped viruses are released when the
infected cell lyses, as a bacterium does at the end of a phage's lytic cycle (see [*How bacteria
copy themselves and change*](../bacteria/bacterial-genetics.qmd#sec-gen-phage)). Lysis kills the
cell, which is one way viral infection damages tissue (see [*Viruses and the
host*](virus-host.qmd#sec-vhost-damage)).

::: {.example}
Influenza virus attaches when haemagglutinin binds sialic acid, a sugar on the surface of airway
epithelial cells. New virions bud from the cell surface and stay stuck to the same sugar until
neuraminidase cuts it, which frees them to infect neighbouring cells.
:::

## From genome to mRNA {#sec-vstr-genomes}

Every virus must present the host cell's ribosomes with mRNA, because the cell has no other way to
make protein. How a virus does so depends on its genome. A single strand of RNA is
**positive-sense** if its sequence is that of an mRNA, so that ribosomes can translate it directly,
and **negative-sense** if it is complementary to mRNA, so that it must be copied before it can be
translated. Human cells make RNA only from DNA and have no enzyme that copies RNA from an RNA
template, so every RNA virus needs its own **RNA-dependent RNA polymerase**, a viral enzyme that
makes RNA from an RNA template.

| Genome | How mRNA is made | What the virus must supply |
|---|---|---|
| Double-stranded DNA; partly double-stranded in hepatitis B virus | Host RNA polymerase transcribes the viral DNA, as it transcribes the cell's own genes | No enzyme for making mRNA; some DNA viruses encode their own DNA polymerase to copy the genome, and hepatitis B virus a reverse transcriptase |
| Positive-sense RNA | The genome is itself an mRNA: host ribosomes translate it as soon as it is uncoated | An RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, translated from the genome, which copies the genome |
| Negative-sense RNA | The viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase transcribes mRNA from the genome | An RNA-dependent RNA polymerase carried inside the virion, because the genome cannot be translated to make one |
| Double-stranded RNA | The viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase transcribes mRNA from the genome | An RNA-dependent RNA polymerase carried inside the virion, because a double-stranded genome cannot be translated |
| Retrovirus: positive-sense RNA copied into DNA | Reverse transcriptase copies the RNA into DNA; integrase joins the DNA into a host chromosome; host RNA polymerase transcribes it | Reverse transcriptase and integrase, carried inside the virion |

Influenza virus has a segmented, negative-sense RNA genome and belongs in the third row. Rotavirus, a
cause of severe diarrhoea in infants and young children, has a double-stranded RNA genome in segments
and belongs in the fourth (see [*Viruses spread by the faecal–oral
route*](enteric-viruses.qmd#sec-entv-rotavirus)). HIV is a retrovirus and belongs in the fifth.

::: {.example}
Influenza virus packages its RNA-dependent RNA polymerase with each of its eight negative-sense
segments, so that mRNA can be made as soon as the segments are uncoated.
:::

A **retrovirus** is an RNA virus that copies its genome into DNA inside the cell, reversing the usual
flow of information from DNA to RNA. The enzyme that makes this copy is **reverse transcriptase**, a
viral DNA polymerase that uses RNA as its template. The viral enzyme integrase then cuts a host
chromosome and joins the viral DNA into it, a step called **integration**. The integrated viral DNA
is a **provirus**: it is part of the cell's genome, transcribed by host RNA polymerase and copied with
the chromosomes each time the cell divides, much like the prophage of a bacteriophage (see [*How
bacteria copy themselves and change*](../bacteria/bacterial-genetics.qmd#sec-gen-phage)). A provirus
that is not being transcribed makes no viral proteins, so neither the immune response nor drugs aimed
at viral enzymes can remove it, and HIV infection persists for life (see [*Viruses and the
host*](virus-host.qmd#sec-vhost-persistence)).

::: {.example}
HIV binds CD4, a protein on the surface of CD4 T cells (lymphocytes that coordinate immune
responses), together with a second receptor, and its envelope fuses with the plasma membrane. Reverse
transcriptase then copies the RNA genome into DNA, and integrase inserts that DNA into a chromosome of
the T cell as a provirus.
:::

Hepatitis B virus also encodes a reverse transcriptase, although its genome is DNA. In the nucleus,
its partly double-stranded DNA genome is completed and then transcribed by host RNA polymerase; in the
cytoplasm, reverse transcriptase copies one of the RNA transcripts back into DNA to make the genomes
of new virions (see [*Blood-borne and sexually transmitted
viruses*](bloodborne-viruses.qmd#sec-bbv-hbv)).

## What a virus has that human cells lack {#sec-vstr-targets}

Selective toxicity, harming the microbe without harming the host, is harder to achieve against a
virus than against a bacterium (see [*How bacteria are built and get
energy*](../bacteria/bacteria-build-energy.qmd#sec-bact-glance)). A virus uses the host cell's
ribosomes, energy and most of its enzymes, and a drug that blocked these would harm the patient's
cells as well. The targets that remain are the few proteins the virus brings or encodes for itself,
which human cells lack or make in a form different enough for a drug to tell them apart.

| Viral enzyme | What it does | Step of the cycle | Anchor virus |
|---|---|---|---|
| RNA-dependent RNA polymerase | Makes RNA from an RNA template, which human cells cannot do | Genome expression and copying | Influenza virus |
| Reverse transcriptase | Copies the RNA genome into DNA | Genome expression and copying | HIV |
| Integrase | Joins the viral DNA into a host chromosome | Genome expression and copying | HIV |
| Protease | Cuts long viral precursor proteins into working proteins, so that new virions become infectious | Assembly and release | HIV |
| Neuraminidase | Cuts sialic acid to free new virions from the cell surface | Release | Influenza virus |

Each of these enzymes is the target of a class of antiviral drugs named after it, such as reverse
transcriptase inhibitors and neuraminidase inhibitors (see [*Detecting viruses and antiviral
targets*](detecting-viruses.qmd#sec-vdet-targets) for where along the cycle each class acts).

::: {.callout-important}
## Do antibacterial drugs act on viruses?
Antibacterial drugs are often expected to help viral infections such as influenza. The expectation is
understandable, because bacterial and viral infections of the airway can produce the same symptoms,
and "antibiotic" is used loosely for any drug against microbes. Antibacterial drugs act on structures
that bacteria have and human cells lack, such as the peptidoglycan wall and 70S ribosomes. A virus has
no wall and uses the host cell's own 80S ribosomes, so these drugs have nothing in it to act on.
:::
